newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank denies report of Duisenberg criticism.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank denies report of Duisenberg criticism.

text.p: Germany's Bundesbank on Sunday denied a report which said it had accused Wim Duisenberg, head of the Dutch central bank and president-designate of the European Monetary Institute, of a breach of trust.

"A report in Sunday's edition of Welt am Sonntag, which suggests criticism of the Dutch central bank by the German Bundesbank is a fiction lacking any basis in fact," a Bundesbank spokesman told Reuters.

The report in the Welt am Sonntag newspaper said the Bundesbank had accused Duisenberg of a breach of trust after Duisenberg was quoted in a magazine interview urging a loose interpretation of the criteria for EMU membership.
"The Bundesbank saw no need to take any position on the comments made in a weekend meeting, as quoted in Welt am Sonntag," the spokesman said.
"The consensus which exists between the Bundesbank and the EMI president designate on the implementation of the Maastricht criteria is unchanged," said the spokesman.

Duisenberg was reported as saying that Luxembourg, Denmark, Ireland and the Netherlands were ready for EMU membership, even though Denmark, Ireland and the Netherlands had not reached the debt criteria laid out in the Maastricht criteria.

The report said Duisenberg thought the debt levels should be allowed reach the required levels at a satisfactory pace and said it would meet the Treaty requirements if they came in under the target in the next ten years.
EU members are scheduled to decide in early 1998 which countries will be in the first wave of monetary union, due to begin in 1999. Their decision will be based on data for 1997.
The target for debt-to-GDP ratio is 60 percent, while the requirement for budget deficits is at or below three percent of gross domestic product.
Germany has traditionally maintained a hard line on strict adherence to the entry criteria. ((--Frankfurt Newsroom +49 69 756525))
